A3.4 Alternative Databases & Data Warehouses HL

Topic A3: Databases | NoSQL, Analytics & Distributed Data

Retrieval Practice

Recall A3.3 (SQL) before moving beyond relational databases.

  1. What does a JOIN do?
  2. What is the difference between DDL and DML?
  3. Why do transactions use COMMIT and ROLLBACK?

Press Down for answers

Answer 1

What does a JOIN do?

It combines rows from two tables using a matching key (primary ↔ foreign key).

Answer 2

What is the difference between DDL and DML?

DDL defines structure (tables). DML queries/changes data (rows).

Answer 3

Why do transactions use COMMIT and ROLLBACK?

To make a set of changes permanent (commit) or undo partial changes if something fails (rollback).

The Big Question HL

🤔 If relational databases are so reliable…

why do companies still build NoSQL systems?

❌ Common misconception: “NoSQL is always better than SQL.”

Different problems need different data models.

✅ Reality: alternatives trade strict consistency for scale, flexibility, or specialized queries.

Your job is to justify the best choice for the scenario.

HL Database approaches

What changes when your data is huge, fast-changing, or relationship-heavy?
ApproachStrengthTypical use
Relationalintegrity + complex joinsbanking, school systems
NoSQLflexible schemas + scaleweb apps, big data
Graphrelationship queriessocial networks, fraud detection
Data warehouseanalytics/reportingbusiness intelligence

HL NoSQL database types

How can data be stored without fixed tables?

Document — store JSON-like documents (e.g., user profiles)

Key–value — fast lookups by key (e.g., caches)

Wide-column — column families for huge, sparse data

Graph — nodes/edges for relationship traversal

Choosing a type

Document: content that varies per record.

Key–value: fastest simple lookups.

Graph: “friends of friends” type queries.

HL Data warehouses

Why store data twice: once for running the business, once for analysing it?

Objective: fast analytics and reporting (trends, dashboards).

Often integrates data from multiple systems (sales, web, support).

Uses ETL to clean/transform data before loading.

OLTP vs OLAP

OLTP: many small updates (transactions).

OLAP: fewer, heavy read queries (analytics).

🧠 Quick Check HL

A retailer wants weekly dashboards showing trends by store, product, and region.

Explain why a data warehouse is usually better than running these queries on the live transactional database.

Warehouses are optimized for OLAP analytics and heavy reads; OLTP systems are optimized for fast transactions.

Separating them protects performance of the live system and supports historical trend analysis.

HL OLAP & data mining

How do businesses turn huge historical data into decisions?

OLAP explores data across dimensions (time, region, product).

Data mining finds patterns (e.g., associations, clusters).

Example questions

“Which products sell together on weekends?”

“Which regions show a rising trend in cancellations?”

🔗 Connection to A4: machine learning often builds on patterns discovered from warehouses and mining pipelines.

HL Distributed databases

How can one “database” live in multiple places at once?

Replication improves availability and read performance.

Sharding (fragmentation) scales by splitting data across servers.

Systems must manage consistency when multiple copies exist.

Some systems accept eventual consistency to stay available during network problems.

🧠 Quick Check HL

A company stores user profiles where each user can have different fields (subscriptions, preferences, devices).

Recommend a database type (relational vs document vs graph) and justify your choice.

Good answer: a document database handles flexible fields well, and scales horizontally for web workloads.

If relationship traversal is central (e.g., “friends of friends”), a graph database may be justified.

Misconception Check HL

True or False: “NoSQL means no structure and no rules.”

False. Many NoSQL systems still use schemas (often flexible) and enforce rules at the application or database level.

NoSQL usually means “not only SQL”: different models designed for different trade-offs.

Key Takeaways HL

  • Alternative databases exist to improve scale, flexibility, or specialized querying.
  • NoSQL includes document, key–value, wide-column, and graph models.
  • Data warehouses support analytics; ETL prepares data for reporting.
  • OLAP explores trends; data mining discovers patterns in large data sets.
  • Distributed databases use replication/sharding and must manage consistency.

Connection: A4 Machine Learning uses data pipelines that often start here (warehousing + mining).
